content.p: In the last hours of 17 July 1992 and the early morning of the 18th, armed men in hoods went through the student and staff housing at La Cantuta, a state teachers' university on the outskirts of Lima. They left with nine students and one professor. For nearly a year the army and the courts said they knew nothing. In July 1993 journalists found burned bones in graves in Cieneguilla, and the case moved from denial to evidence.

Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission concluded that the ten were executed without trial by agents of the state, and that the investigation was deliberately obstructed during Fujimori's government through laws and court decisions meant to shield those responsible. The abductions were the work of the Colina Group, an army intelligence detachment. A military court convicted some of its members in 1994 and an amnesty freed them in 1995. Fujimori himself was convicted in 2009 as the indirect perpetrator of the La Cantuta killings and of the earlier Barrios Altos massacre. In December 2023 he walked out of prison on a humanitarian pardon, against the wishes of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights and of the victims' families.

La Cantuta, formally the Enrique Guzmán y Valle National University of Education, was one of the state universities that Shining Path had tried to recruit in. The Truth Commission wrote that the presence of students linked to the guerrillas fed a wider prejudice against thousands of students at national universities, who were routinely detained as suspects. According to the Commission, a military document prepared as part of the counter-insurgency strategy described La Cantuta as a centre for military preparation.

On 21 May 1991 Fujimori visited the campus and, in the Commission's account, was driven out by a violent reaction from students. The next day troops took over La Cantuta and San Marcos University, and 56 students were detained at La Cantuta, three of them among the nine later abducted. The army set up a post on campus called the Civic Action Base and imposed a curfew and controls on entering and leaving. The National Intelligence Service, the Commission notes, also placed agents in the universities to report on students and lecturers.

Students complained about the soldiers well before the abductions. On 29 May 1992 the boarders' committee told the university's rector that on 24 May between 20 and 25 hooded, armed and drunken soldiers had come to the residences and threatened to force the doors, as recorded by the Inter-American Court. In July, student groups sent another note about soldiers bursting into a Teachers' Day ceremony with firearms.
content.h2: Tarata Street and the Colina Group
content.p: Peru was in the middle of a war with Shining Path. Fujimori had dissolved Congress and taken control of the judiciary in April 1992, and the Truth Commission counts dozens of car bombs in Lima in 1991 and 1992. On 16 July 1992 two vehicles carrying more than half a tonne of explosives went off on Tarata Street in Miraflores. The Commission records 22 dead and more than 100 injured.

The Instituto de Estudios Peruanos describes the La Cantuta operation as a reprisal for that bombing, based on intelligence that some of the students had taken part in it. A Peruvian tribunal later found that none of the victims was linked to Shining Path (see below).

The Colina Group, according to the prosecutors' findings reported by the Truth Commission, began in 1991 as a command of army intelligence agents formed under the army's intelligence directorate, as part of a clandestine strategy against subversion. The Inter-American Court, relying on the Commission and on the admissions of the Peruvian state, described a group tied to the National Intelligence Service whose operations were known to the president and the army commander. Its members drew their army pay, operating expenses and cash bonuses. Its first attributed attack in Lima was the killing of fifteen people at Barrios Altos in November 1991.

The Truth Commission places the raid between late on 17 July and the early hours of the 18th, with Colina members working alongside soldiers from the base on the campus and some fifty witnesses present. The Inter-American Court, summarising the proven facts, says the men were hooded, wore black turtlenecks and entered the residences of students and staff. They made the students lie face down on the floor. One soldier, whom the students identified as a Lieutenant Medina, lifted each student's head by the hair and picked out those on a list.

At the staff housing the troops climbed the yard wall of Professor Hugo Muñoz Sánchez's home and forced the service entrance. In the account the Court recites from the petitioners, he was gagged, hooded with a black cloth and dragged out of the house, while others searched his bedroom and kept his wife in it. Nine students disappeared with him. Their names are in the details above; they include Bertila Lozano and Dora Oyague, as well as Luis Enrique Ortiz, Armando Amaro, Robert Teodoro, Heráclides Pablo, Felipe Flores, Marcelino Rosales and Juan Mariños.
The Instituto de Estudios Peruanos says they were taken to open ground in Cieneguilla, shot and buried. Relatives had no idea where they had been taken, according to the Court's findings.

Within days families filed habeas corpus petitions. The Inter-American Court summarises how they failed. A judge dismissed the petition for Dora Oyague on 5 August 1992, stating that she had in no way been detained by the military and that no operation had been ordered at the university. A second petition was dismissed the same day after the head of the Second Military Region denied ordering or knowing of any operation. In a third, the army commander, General Nicolás de Bari Hermoza Ríos, denied that anyone had been detained and cited national security as a reason not to identify the troops on the campus. An appeals panel in February 1993 noted "serious procedural irregularities" but the proceedings were closed.

The press kept the case alive. The Truth Commission records that in December 1992 the magazine Sí reported, from anonymous sources, that Barrios Altos and La Cantuta were the work of members of the intelligence service. The former defence and interior ministers and the head of the intelligence service responded by filing a complaint against the magazine's director, Ricardo Uceda. Journalists at Caretas also voiced suspicions of paramilitary involvement and, the Commission says, received anonymous death threats.
content.h2: Congress, a general's letter and the army's answer
content.p: On 2 April 1993 Congressman Henry Pease told the chamber he had found an anonymous document, purporting to come from army officers, saying the professor and nine students had been killed by an army commando with the knowledge of senior commanders. The Truth Commission calls the group behind it COMACA; the Inter-American Court calls it "León Dormido". Congress created an investigating committee.

The army moved to take the case into its own courts. On 15 April 1993 its general command filed a complaint with the Supreme Council of Military Justice. When Hermoza Ríos testified before the committee on 20 April, he denied any army role and said the accusations came from opponents of the government's pacification policy who wanted to damage the army's prestige. The next day the army issued a statement backing him while tanks moved to the armed forces' joint command building, which the Court describes as a show of support. The Commission calls it a parade of tanks and troops through Lima's streets, a gesture of intimidation.

In May 1993 the third most senior officer in the army, General Rodolfo Robles Espinoza, made a handwritten letter public. He wrote that the La Cantuta crime "was carried out by a special intelligence detachment operating under direct orders from Presidential Advisor and virtual head of the SIN, Vladimiro Montesinos," and that the Commander General of the army always knew and approved such actions. Fujimori backed Hermoza Ríos and Montesinos. According to the Commission, the military court put Robles himself on trial for insulting the nation and the armed forces.

On 26 June 1993 the Democratic Constituent Congress voted 39 to 13 against the committee's majority report, which had presumed army officers criminally liable, and adopted the minority report, which found no evidence that the army or the intelligence service was responsible.

On 8 July 1993 journalists from Sí found clandestine graves in the Chavilca gorge at Cieneguilla; on 12 July the magazine published a sketch and gave it to a prosecutor. Víctor Cubas Villanueva, the prosecutor in charge, found four graves containing mostly charred bones, spent cartridges, scraps of clothing and two sets of keys. On 13 July the national anti-terrorism police said they had seized a handwritten note and sketch of the graves from alleged Shining Path members, and named a man as the author of the sketch, and ordered a handwriting analysis to back the claim. The keys told a different story: in August 1993 an operation at the student residences confirmed they belonged to Armando Amaro Cóndor and Juan Mariños Figueroa.

Experts concluded that the remains in the Cieneguilla graves were a second burial: the bodies had been dug up, burned while decomposing and reburied. Part of a young woman's skull showed a bullet wound at the back of the head. Relatives identified clothing belonging to Amaro, Mariños, Teodoro and Pablo, and a dental examination established that some teeth were Bertila Lozano's. Further graves were found at Huachipa after Sí published new information on 2 November (the Court's judgment says 1995 in one paragraph and 1993 in another; the Truth Commission says 1993); one skeleton, of a man aged 22 to 24 killed by gunshots to the head, was identified through clothing and shoes by Gisela Ortiz Perea as those of her brother Luis Enrique.

By the time of the Inter-American Court's 2006 judgment only Lozano and Ortiz had been identified from remains; eight others were still counted as disappeared. A tombstone in the El Angel cemetery lists all ten names, though a visiting fellow of The Advocacy Project noted in 2010 that it holds only fragments of some of the victims and that some bodies had never been recovered.

After the graves were found, the ordinary prosecutor filed a criminal complaint on 16 December 1993 against a group of army officers and non-commissioned officers, and a criminal court in Lima opened proceedings. The military prosecutor challenged its jurisdiction. On 3 February 1994 the Supreme Court's criminal chamber split three to two over which court should hear the case. Within days Congress passed, and Fujimori signed, Law 26,291, which let a simple majority of the chamber settle such conflicts by secret ballot. On 11 February the chamber sent the case to the military court.

On 21 February 1994 the military court convicted Majors Santiago Martín Rivas and Carlos Pichilingue Guevara of abuse of authority, abduction, forced disappearance and murder, and sentenced them to 20 years. Three non-commissioned officers received 15 years. Brigade General Juan Rivero Lazo and Colonel Federico Navarro Pérez were convicted only of negligence and given five and four years; they were acquitted of the other charges for insufficient evidence. The court also ordered reparations and left open proceedings against a lieutenant who was missing. A separate military case against Hermoza Ríos, General Luis Pérez Documet and Montesinos was dismissed in August 1994 for insufficient evidence.

On 14 June 1995 Congress passed Law 26,479, amnestying military, police and civilian personnel for human rights violations since May 1980, and ordering immediate release of those held and closure of pending cases. Two days later the military council applied it to the La Cantuta convicts and ordered them freed. Law 26,492, passed on 28 June, said the amnesty was mandatory for judges and covered all acts connected with the fight against terrorism up to 14 June 1995. In October 2001 the Supreme Council of Military Justice declared the June 1995 amnesty decision null.

CEJIL, the legal group that represented relatives before the Inter-American Court, says the case was reopened in the ordinary courts in 2000 and that proceedings against the accused began in 2003, while a Truth and Reconciliation Commission created in 2001 reported in 2003. In 2003 and 2004 the Supreme Court convicted the military judges who had dismissed the case against the alleged masterminds of personal cover-up and criminal association, according to the Inter-American Court.

The Inter-American Court issued its judgment on 29 November 2006. Peru had acquiesced to the claims and partly acknowledged its responsibility. The Court found unanimously that the state had violated the victims' rights to life, humane treatment and personal liberty, and the relatives' rights to humane treatment, a fair trial and judicial protection. It ordered Peru to complete the pending investigations and trials without delay. CEJIL says the ruling declared the amnesty laws contrary to the American Convention and therefore invalid.

Human Rights Watch recorded that, after Congress lifted Fujimori's immunity, Peru's attorney general formally accused him of murder, grievous injury and "disappearances" over Barrios Altos and La Cantuta. He had resigned by fax from Japan in November 2000, Al Jazeera notes, and was arrested in Chile in November 2005, then extradited to Peru in 2007. His trial before the Supreme Court's special criminal chamber began on 10 December 2007.

On 7 April 2009 the three judges, led by César San Martín, unanimously convicted him as the indirect perpetrator of aggravated murder in both massacres, which they called crimes against humanity, and of the kidnapping of the journalist Gustavo Gorriti and the businessman Samuel Dyer. El Comercio reported that the court found all four charges proven beyond reasonable doubt and sentenced him to 25 years, counted from his detention in Chile, so that he would leave prison on 10 February 2032. El Comercio called it the first conviction of an elected Latin American former head of state for human rights abuses by a court in his own country. Fujimori appealed the verdict.

The ruling also stated explicitly that the 29 people harmed in the two cases, including the La Cantuta students and professor, had no links to Shining Path's terrorist actions. The families welcomed it. Gisela Ortiz said it dignified the memory of their relatives, and Raida Cóndor, the mother of Armando Amaro, said she could now lift her head and say her son was Armando Amaro Cóndor. The Fujimorista congresswoman Cecilia Chacón said the court had exceeded its role in declaring the victims innocent, though she said she could not say whether they were terrorists.

On 24 December 2017 President Pedro Pablo Kuczynski pardoned Fujimori on humanitarian grounds, some twelve years into the sentence. The decision came a few days before a congressional motion to remove Kuczynski failed, when members of the party of Fujimori's daughter Keiko voted against it, as the legal commentary at EJIL: Talk! noted. On 30 May 2018 the Inter-American Court asked Peru to consider a judicial review, weighing victims' access to justice and Fujimori's health. NPR reports that Peru's Supreme Court overturned the pardon in 2018 under pressure from the Court and ordered him back to prison.

On 17 March 2022 the Constitutional Tribunal ruled that the pardon should take effect. On 7 April 2022 the Inter-American Court ordered Peru not to implement the release. Then, on 4 December 2023, the tribunal ordered his immediate release, saying that although the seriousness of the crimes was evident it could not ignore the pardon. (The ICJ and the IACHR date the ruling 4 December; NPR and Al Jazeera, reporting on the 6th, place it on "Tuesday", the 5th.) The Inter-American Court asked Peru on 5 December to refrain from implementing it, but Fujimori, then 85, left Lima's Barbadillo prison on 6 December. His children Keiko and Kenji greeted him outside.

The International Commission of Jurists called the release unlawful and an affront to victims. The IACHR said it did not comply with Peru's international obligations. Gisela Ortiz told The Associated Press, "We live in an orphanhood because we do not have institutions of any kind capable of defending us." Carmen Oyague, whose daughter Dora Oyague Fierro has never been found, had told a visitor years earlier: "We want to continue fighting because we want to know what happened to our family members."
